narrative:
The model determined that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influence, and both pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, well below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic performance that it associates with higher risk of not passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction slightly toward passing. At 3.20 it sits almost exactly at the average of accepted students, so the model saw this as a neutral-to-positive signal.

Your family income bracket (middle) was the third most influential feature and also nudged the outcome modestly toward success, though not enough to overcome the academic ranking signals.

In short, the model concluded that your class standing over time raised the risk of bar failure above the level the school was willing to accept.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record. Improving your class rank in future semesters, or supplementing your application with a strong LSAT retake and additional evidence of bar-exam readiness, would directly address the factors that led to this denial.
